analysis.one_liner: Taxes big corporations extra on profits when CEO pay dwarfs typical worker pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new tax on top of regular corporate income taxes for companies with more than $1 billion in yearly revenue whose chief executive earns more than 30 times what the typical employee makes. The extra tax starts at 2% of profits and climbs to 10% as the gap between the CEO's pay and the median worker's pay grows. Its sponsors' aim was to give corporations a financial reason to narrow that pay gap.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, employees of very large corporations would have benefited in two ways: companies would have had a direct financial incentive to raise the median worker's pay (the single most effective way to shrink the measured ratio and cut the tax), and the surtax revenue would come from roughly 2% to 10% of the profits of corporations with extreme pay gaps, money available to the Treasury for other priorities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees of giant corporations with extreme pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: It creates a direct financial penalty for large pay gaps: a corporation with over $1 billion in gross revenue whose highest-paid officer earns more than 30 times the median employee's salary would pay an added tax of 2% of taxable income, rising in steps to 10% if the CEO earns 1,000 or more times the median, applying to tax years starting after December 31, 2019.

The simplest way for a covered company to reduce the tax is to raise its median employee salary or lower executive pay, so the tax is designed to push money toward ordinary workers at the biggest firms.

The measure is aimed at a widely noted problem: at many large public companies the chief executive now earns hundreds of times what the typical employee does, and the bill would make that gap itself a taxable cost.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations with over $1 billion in gross revenues and CEO-to-median-pay ratios above 3,000% would pay the surtax. More broadly, their shareholders would absorb it through lower after-tax profits, and the companies' executives and boards would face pressure to restructure compensation. Some costs could ultimately be passed on to consumers through prices, though the bill's supporters argued the point is to change pay practices rather than collect revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios

drawbacks.text: The tax measures only wages and salary. Corporate executives are typically paid largely in stock, and the bill defines officer pay using wage rules that capture W-2 compensation, so a CEO with a modest salary and a huge stock package could keep the ratio low and avoid the surtax entirely.

The ratio counts the corporation's employees, so a company could lower its measured gap by outsourcing low-wage jobs to contractors rather than by raising anyone's pay, rewarding restructuring instead of better wages.

It had no cosponsors, which signals that even senators sympathetic to the pay-gap concern saw design problems or saw no path for the bill; a tax on paper profits of a subset of large corporations invites accounting responses and enforcement complexity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — narrowing the pay gap between executives and workers at the largest companies — addresses a real and widely shared concern, but the tool chosen is narrow and porous: it only covers W-2 salary, ignores stock-based executive pay, counts only direct employees, and exempts companies under $1 billion in revenue, so many of the pay arrangements it targets would fall outside its net. As a revenue measure it would raise comparatively little; its real function would be as an incentive, and only for companies whose pay structures the formula actually catches.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on July 30, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the committee that handles tax legislation.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021.

Because a tax bill can only start in the House under the Constitution, a Senate tax bill typically needs a House companion to move; no companion was reported for this bill, and the two actions in its history are introduction and referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay gaps, and the executives whose compensation packages were untouched, are better off because the bill never advanced; workers at those companies gained nothing from its failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations and highly paid executives

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to the Finance Committee; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

against.name: Large corporations with high CEO pay ratios
against.role: Companies that would have owed the new surtax
against.what_they_did: No organized support for the bill appears in the record; the measure targeted their tax liability and compensation practices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors of either party; the Republican-run Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, so it never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Large corporations (over $1 billion gross revenue) with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios
industries.note: These companies would owe an added tax of 2% to 10% of taxable income based on how far their CEO's pay exceeds the median employee's pay, giving them a reason to raise worker pay or restructure compensation to avoid it. Their financial interest in the bill runs against the workers the bill tries to help.

Executives at covered firms would face pressure on their pay packages, since their compensation relative to the median employee is the trigger for the tax. The bill only counts W-2 wages, so executives paid mainly in stock could largely shield themselves.

industries.industry: Payroll, tax compliance, and accounting services
industries.note: A new corporate tax keyed to pay ratios would require new calculations and planning, creating work for tax advisers and payroll systems at affected firms.
